questions.q: Given below are two statements: Statement I: Bromination of phenol in solvent with low polarity such as CHCl3 or CS2 requires Lewis acid catalyst. Statement II: The Lewis acid catalyst polarises the bromine to generate Br+. Choose the correct answer.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
questions.explain: The question is whether phenol needs a Lewis acid for bromination. The OH group donates by +M, so the ring is so electron rich that plain Br2 can attack it with no catalyst. So Statement I is false. A Lewis acid does polarise Br-Br to give a Br+ like electrophile, which is what benzene needs, so Statement II is a true fact. Statement I false, Statement II true.

questions.q: Phenol treated with chloroform in presence of sodium hydroxide, which is further hydrolysed in presence of an acid, results in:
questions.explain: This is the Reimer-Tiemann reaction. NaOH turns phenol into phenoxide, which is far more electron rich, and CHCl3 with base forms dichlorocarbene (:CCl2), a strong electrophile. The carbene attacks the ortho carbon and leaves CHCl2, which hydrolyses to CHO. After acid work-up you get 2-hydroxybenzaldehyde. Salicylic acid would need CO2 (Kolbe), and the diols have no source of oxygen in these reagents.

questions.q: The difference in the reaction of phenol with bromine in chloroform and bromine in water medium is due to:
questions.explain: The reagent is the same, so the difference has to come from the medium. In water, which is polar, phenol partly ionises to phenoxide, a much stronger activator, and water also helps polarise Br2. So all the ortho and para positions react and you get 2,4,6-tribromophenol. In CHCl3 or CS2 (low polarity) there is almost no ionisation, so only a mono-bromo ortho/para product forms. So it is the polarity of the solvent.
